section: Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
text:
Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
PubMed alerts are a reasonable starting point, but they have a key limitation: they give you a flat, unsorted list. If you set up an alert for “inflammatory bowel disease,” every matching paper arrives in the same inbox pile - therapeutics next to epidemiology next to basic science - and you still have to read through everything to find what’s relevant to your work.
IBD LitMonitor takes a different approach. Instead of delivering a raw feed, it organizes papers into sub-fields so you can go straight to the topic area you care about and skip the rest. Each category is collapsible, so browsing the day’s literature takes minutes rather than a lengthy inbox triage.

Shorter infliximab infusion times without premedication do not increase adverse reactions.  Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition  |  2026-11-02



Infliximab (IFX) infusions for paediatric inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are resource intensive and time-intrusive on patient’s lives. Longer infusion times and administering routine pre-medications compound such timelines, despite limited supporting evidence. This study investigated whether discontinuing routine premedication and shortening IFX infusion durations increased infusion reaction rates. This retrospective comparative cohort study analysed data from 1083 IFX infusions (369 patients) at a single national referral centre. It compared a cohort receiving routine dual hydrocortisone/chlorphenamine premedication with longer infusion times (2.5 h induction/90 min maintenance; Group A) with a subsequent cohort without universal premedication and shorter infusions (2 h induction/60 min maintenance; Group B). The primary outcome was the rate of acute infusion reactions; secondary outcomes included anti-IFX antibody formation and rates of post-infusion reactions. There were 346 infusions in Group A and 737 infusions in Group B. Shorter infusions and omitting routine premedication did not increase acute infusion reaction rates (Group A: 1.5/100 vs. Group B: 1.1/100 infusions, p = 0.6; odds ratio 0.75 [0.24, 2.3]). Universal premedication neither reduced early anti-IFX antibody positivity by first maintenance dose (n = 51; 33% vs. 17%, p = 0.23) nor overall antibody prevalence (31% vs. 37%, p = 0.164). No reactions occurred during extended post-infusion observation periods in either group. Neither longer infusion times, universal pre-medication nor prolonged post-infusion observation significantly enhanced patient safety or reduced anti-drug antibody formation. Practice modification could reduce treatment burden for patients and families and improve healthcare efficiency.


Lane M, Almaiman A, Obasi S, Broderick A, Bourke B, Dunne C, Fitzpatrick E, Stenke E, Stallard L, Quinn S


DOI: 10.1002/jpn3.70642  |  View on PubMed →





A cross-sectional study on pharmacotherapy and predictors of clinical remission in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.  Indian journal of pharmacology  |  2026-11-02



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, progressive, and disabling disorder that includes ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease, characterized by periods of remission and relapse. Pharmacological management is the primary treatment option with the goal to induce mucosal healing and reduce relapse rates. The main objective of the present study was to determine the pattern of pharmacotherapy and to evaluate the factors that predict clinical remission in patients with IBD. A cross-sectional analysis was conducted involving fifty participants diagnosed with IBD. All the participants met predefined study inclusion criteria and voluntarily provided written informed consent. Data encompassing patient demographics, clinical parameters, prescribed medications, and ADRs were collected. The disease activity was evaluated using Simple Clinical Colitis Activity Index/Harvey-Bradshaw Index score. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analysis was done to assess predictors of clinical remission. The commonly prescribed drugs were mesalamine in 72%, steroids in 50%, and azathioprine in 46% patients. 30% patients had an ADR to the prescribed drug; the most common ADR was anemia and pancytopenia with azathioprine use. 52% patients were in clinical remission. Univariate analysis identified medication adherence as a significant predictor, which was confirmed on multivariate analysis. Patient’s adherent to medication were 32 times more likely to be in remission compared to nonadherent patients. Mesalamine and azathioprine were the most commonly prescribed monotherapy drugs. The most frequently prescribed combination therapies were mesalamine in conjunction with either steroids or azathioprine. Adherence to medication was the only factor statistically significantly linked to achieving clinical remission of the disease.


Shivanna A, Panchaksharimath P


DOI: 10.4103/ijp.ijp_137_26  |  View on PubMed →





S1P receptors in ulcerative colitis: spotlight on etrasimod.Review  Expert opinion on pharmacotherapy  |  2026-11-01



Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with a rising global incidence. Small molecules have transformed the treatment of UC. Specifically, sphingosine‑1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulators are a newly available and expanding therapeutic option for patients with UC. This review analyzes the biology, efficacy, and safety of S1P receptor modulators. A literature search in PubMed regarding clinical studies published up to 1 June 2026, involving S1P receptor modulators in UC was analyzed. Clinical trial data and real-world evidence for approved S1P receptor modulators (ozanimod and etrasimod) and investigational agents (tamuzimod, mocravimod, and amiselimod) in UC treatment were gathered. Ozanimod and etrasimod both demonstrated superior efficacy over placebo in moderately to severely active UC. Both agents showed greater efficacy in biologic-naïve patients compared with biologic-exposed populations. Meta-analyses favored S1P receptor modulators over other UC therapies, particularly for inducing histologic improvement. Commonly reported adverse effects of S1P receptor modulators include elevated liver enzymes and transient asymptomatic bradycardia. Serious adverse events, including macular edema and severe infections, are rare, with infection rates comparable to those of placebo in the clinical trials. S1P receptor modulators represent a new and promising oral class of treatment for UC, showing effective results with a manageable safety profile. They are especially beneficial for patients with moderate disease severity and serve as an important option for those transitioning from traditional to advanced therapies. Although these agents have some unique safety concerns, most are mild and reversible.


Shafrir A, Allen A, Rubin DT


DOI: 10.1080/14656566.2026.2751570  |  View on PubMed →





Forced degradation study of etrasimod: Structural elucidation and transformation pathways of its major degradation products.  Journal of pharmaceutical sciences  |  2026-11-01



Etrasimod is a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1P1) receptor modulator and has been used for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis. Understanding its chemical degradation behaviors is important for evaluation of intrinsic stability and degradation impurities. Herein, the degradation chemistry of solid etrasimod was systematically investigated under ICH-recommended stress conditions. Eight degradation products were detected by using reversed-phase HPLC, and three major products (DP-6, DP-4, and DP-2) was isolated and structurally elucidated by LC-MS combined with multidimensional NMR spectroscopy. DP-6 was assigned as an oxygenated lactone-containing degradation product, DP-4 as a ring-expanded dicarbonyl product, and DP-2 as an open-chain succinic acid derivative. Time-dependent transformation experiments demonstrated the conversion of DP-6 to DP-4 under oxidative conditions and DP-4 to DP-2 under alkaline conditions. These experimentally established transformation relationships, together with the structural information obtained for the major degradation products, support an interconnected degradation pathways involving oxidative transformation and subsequent alkaline hydrolysis. Overall, this study provides experimentally supported insights into the degradation chemistry and transformation relationships of etrasimod, which may facilitate the identification and monitoring of degradation impurities, the assessment of drug-substance stability, and the development of appropriate impurity control strategies during pharmaceutical development.


Qiu S, Jian R, Chen Y, Huang K, Zhou Z, Fan J


DOI: 10.1016/j.xphs.2026.104574  |  View on PubMed →





Anti-TNF Therapy Is Associated With Browning- and Immune-Related Changes in Creeping Fat in Crohn’s Disease.Observational study★  United European gastroenterology journal  |  2026-11



Creeping fat (CrF) in Crohn’s disease (CD) is a metabolically active perilesional adipose tissue involved in intestinal inflammation. Whether biological therapies modify its browning-associated phenotype remains largely unexplored. We investigated whether anti-TNF treatment is associated with changes in browning-, mitochondrial biogenesis- and immune-related pathways in CrF and whether similar molecular changes occur following ex vivo infliximab exposure. Two independent human cohorts were analysed. (1) Observational cohort: CrF biopsies from anti-TNF-treated and anti-TNF-naïve CD patients (n = 14 and n = 19, respectively) were analysed for metabolic and inflammatory gene and protein expression. AdMSCs and mature CrF-derived adipocytes were isolated, and UCP1 protein abundance was assessed by immunohistochemistry and western blotting. (2) Ex vivo cohort: Paired CrF explants from anti-TNF-naïve patients with CD undergoing surgery were cultured with or without infliximab (5 mg/kg-equivalent, 24 h) and analysed by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemistry. Anti-TNF-treated patients showed higher UCP1 expression in CrF at mRNA and protein levels. CrF-derived mature adipocytes from treated patients exhibited increased expression of browning-/thermogenesis- and mitochondrial biogenesis-associated genes, together with reduced selected pro-inflammatory markers. AdMSCs also showed exploratory differences in their conditioned-medium protein profile, although no protein remained significant after FDR correction. Ex vivo infliximab exposure was associated with changes in selected browning-, mitochondrial biogenesis- and immune-related markers. Together, the observational and ex vivo findings identify CrF as an anti-TNF-responsive immunometabolic compartment in CD, characterised by coordinated browning-, mitochondrial biogenesis- and immune-related molecular changes. Functional studies are needed to establish the metabolic significance of these changes.


Monfort-Ferré D, Ginés I, Cepero C, Cabré L, Caro A, Menacho M, Gené M, Garcia M, Lahoz MDC, Mañas MJ


DOI: 10.1002/ueg2.70320  |  View on PubMed →





Safety of Janus kinase inhibitors, ustekinumab, and anti-interleukin-23 in older patients with immune-mediated diseases.Review★  Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association  |  2026-10-31



Data on the safety of newer advanced therapies (AT) for immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) remain limited in older patients, and how the underlying IMID type influences treatment safety is unknown. We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase for studies evaluating the safety of anti-IL12/23 and -IL23 agents, and JAKi in older patients with IMIDs, including inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and psoriasis. Eligible studies included patients who initiated therapy at age ≥50 years and reported outcomes in comparison with (1) younger patients receiving the same therapy, (2) older patients receiving non-AT, or (3) older patients receiving a different AT. Data on infections, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), venous thromboembolism (VTE), malignancy, and mortality were extracted. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model. Seventy-nine studies were included. Compared to other AT, JAKi were associated with a higher risk of infections (OR 1.38; 95% CI, 1.22-1.55) and serious infections (1.27; 1.06-1.52). No increase in MACE, VTE, or malignancy risk was seen overall. Among adults > 60 years, there was an increased risk of VTE in rheumatologic cohorts (3.28; 1.16-9.27) that was absent in IBD (0.99; 0.58-1.70) (p for difference = 0.045). Compared with anti-TNF, Anti-IL-12/23 and -IL-23 agents had a lower risk of serious infections (0.76; 0.68-0.84). In older patients with IMIDs, anti-IL-12/23 and -IL-23 agents had lower serious infection risk while JAKi had an increased risk. JAKi showed a possible disease-specific thromboembolic signal in rheumatologic but not IBD cohorts.


Le Cosquer G, Ranjan MK, Kochar B, Faye AS, Singh S, Ananthakrishnan AN


DOI: 10.1016/j.cgh.2026.10.017  |  View on PubMed →





Vedolizumab use for severe chronic enterocolitis in a child with Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome: A case report.  JPGN reports  |  2026-10-29



We report a patient with Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome (HHS), a telomere biology disorder, who developed severe chronic enterocolitis with inflammatory bowel disease-like features. Vedolizumab led to improvement in stool frequency, reduced fecal calprotectin, and clinical remission without infectious complications. Remission was maintained with vedolizumab monotherapy for 2 years after discontinuation of budesonide and parenteral nutrition. This report highlights vedolizumab as a potentially safe therapeutic option for enterocolitis in HHS, emphasizing the value of gut-selective therapy when systemic immunosuppression is risky. Further studies are needed to establish the long-term efficacy and safety of vedolizumab in patients with telomere biology disorders.


Chiba Y, Takahashi M, Yoshida T, Tagane S, Shiohata T, Miura S, Akasaka M


DOI: 10.1002/jpr3.70291  |  View on PubMed →





Comparing real-world continuous clinical remission rates of anti-tumor necrosis factor, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, tofacitinib, and upadacitinib in ulcerative colitis.★  Inflammatory bowel diseases  |  2026-10-29



Multiple advanced therapies are available for moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (UC), but comparative efficacy data are limited. We compared the 1-year efficacy and safety of 7 therapies: the anti-tumor necrosis factor agents infliximab, adalimumab, and golimumab (GLM); the anti-integrin vedolizumab (VDZ); the anti-interleukin-12/23 ustekinumab (UST); and the JAK inhibitors tofacitinib (TOF) and upadacitinib (UPA). In a retrospective, multicenter, propensity score-matched study, all UC patients treated with the 7 advanced therapies between 2014 and 2024 were included. The primary endpoint was the 1-year rate of continuous clinical remission (CCR) for each drug (defined as the induction and maintenance of steroid-free clinical remission, without the need for drug optimization or additional therapy due to relapse, with no adverse events requiring drug discontinuation). A total of 1406 patients were included (VDZ = 376, infliximab = 341, adalimumab = 207, UST = 150, GLM = 114, TOF = 103, UPA = 115). Excluding UPA from the overall population comparison as it was used only in bio-exposed patients, UST achieved the highest CCR, with GLM the lowest. UST appeared the most effective therapy in bio-naive patients, whereas other biologics achieved similar CCR rates. As second-line therapy, UPA achieved the highest CCR, followed by UST. As third-line therapy, UPA outperformed UST, VDZ, and TOF. UST was associated with the lowest rates of adverse events. Although UPA was associated with the highest rates of adverse events, drug withdrawal was low. In this large multicenter observational cohort, UST was more effective than anti-tumor necrosis factor agents and VDZ as both first- and second-line therapy. In bio-exposed patients, UPA was the most effective advanced therapy.


Cassinotti A, Saibeni S, Cannatelli R, Michelon M, Maconi G, Caprioli F, Lepore F, Lo Bello A, Annunziata ML, Zammarchi I


DOI: 10.1093/ibd/izag229  |  View on PubMed →





Real-world success of de-escalating upadacitinib induction dosing in ulcerative colitis is predicted by steroid-free clinical and biochemical remission, not induction duration.  Crohn’s & colitis 360  |  2026-10-29



Data guiding upadacitinib dose de-escalation in ulcerative colitis (UC) are limited. We evaluated factors associated with UC-related complications (UCRC) after upadacitinib was reduced from 45 mg daily. This retrospective study included adults with UC at a tertiary center who underwent upadacitinib de-escalation (4/2022-11/2025). The primary outcome was a 12-month composite of UCRC (upadacitinib re-escalation or discontinuation, new systemic steroids, new advanced therapy, hospitalization, or colectomy). Predictors of UCRC after de-escalation were assessed using Cox proportional hazards modeling, including steroid-free clinical remission (SFCR), defined as a stool frequency subscore of 0 or 1 and a rectal bleeding subscore of 0 without systemic steroid use, and biochemical remission, defined as a fecal calprotectin (FC) < 150 μg/g or a C-reactive protein (CRP) < 5 mg/L when FC was unavailable. Optimal CRP and FC cut points were identified via ROC curves. Among 70 patients, 25 (35.7%) experienced UCRC (median follow-up 56 weeks). Induction duration, prior advanced therapy exposure, and endoscopic severity did not differ significantly between those with and without UCRC. Patients without UCRC were more likely to have achieved SFCR (51.1% vs 20.0%, P=.01) and biochemical remission (53.3% vs 28.0%, P=.04) prior to de-escalation, with lower median CRP (0.8 vs 1.5 mg/L, P=.04) and FC (79.5 vs 208.0 μg/g, P=.03). In multivariable analysis, achieving SFCR (aHR 0.33, 95% CI, 0.12-0.91) and biochemical remission (aHR 0.34, 95% CI, 0.13-0.85) independently predicted lower UCRC risk, and achieving both conferred additional UCAE-free survival benefit. Optimal cut points predicting UCRC were CRP > 12.7 mg/L (sensitivity 40%, specificity 93%) and FC > 58.7 μg/g (sensitivity 100%, specificity 47%). SFCR and biochemical remission prior to upadacitinib de-escalation, but not induction duration, predict lower UCRC risk. Upadacitinib de-escalation should be guided by response assessment rather than a predetermined induction duration.


Dalal RM, Rotondo-Trivette S, Mason AR, Leveille L, Yin J, Missi C, Boktor M, Fudman DI


DOI: 10.1093/crocol/otag111  |  View on PubMed →





Filgotinib in the treatment of ulcerative colitis: lessons learned from randomized trial to real-world studies.Review  Expert opinion on pharmacotherapy  |  2026-10-29



Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic relapsing inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) of the colon whose treatment has evolved with novel targeted therapies. Filgotinib (FILGO) is a small molecule that preferentially inhibits Janus kinase 1 (JAK1). The SELECTION trial established the efficacy of FILGO for induction and maintenance of remission in UC, and subsequent real-world studies have confirmed its effectiveness. However, real-world evidence remains limited by relatively small sample sizes and short follow-up periods. Several studies have also explored the ability of FILGO to improve health-related quality of life (HRQoL). This review examines and summarizes current evidence and recent advances regarding filgotinib as a therapeutic option for UC, including efficacy, safety, and real-world effectiveness. PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from database inception through June 2026, supplemented by screening the reference lists of identified articles. FILGO is a Janus kinase inhibitor (JAKi) with a favorable efficacy and effectiveness profile, as demonstrated by pivotal trials and real-world (RW) studies. Available evidence also suggests a favorable safety profile within the JAK inhibitor class, although randomized head-to-head comparisons are lacking. Further long-term RW studies are needed to confirm these findings and refine the positioning of FILGO in clinical practice.


Mocci G, Orrù G, Onidi FM, Usai Satta P, Tursi A


DOI: 10.1080/14656566.2026.2750245  |  View on PubMed →





Severe peripheral oedema temporally associated with accelerated infliximab induction for acute severe ulcerative colitis.  BMJ case reports  |  2026-10-29



Abstract not available.


Gontar A, Hafez Y, Shmais M


DOI: 10.1136/bcr-2026-275021  |  View on PubMed →





Severe Hypertriglyceridemia Associated With Acute Pancreatitis in a Patient on Risankizumab.Case report  ACG case reports journal  |  2026-10-28



Hypertriglyceridemia is a frequent condition, and it has many causes including obesity, hypothyroidism, and some medication. Allobaculum stercoricanis and Its Postbiotics Alleviate Dextran Sulfate Sodium (DSS)-Induced Colitis through the Regulation of theTLR4/NF-κB Signaling Pathway.  Journal of agricultural and food chemistry  |  2026-11



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic intestinal disorder that has become a global public health concern. Postbiotics offer advantages in biosafety and reproducibility over probiotics. Here, we demonstrated that live Allobaculum stercoricanis (A. stercoricanis) and its two postbiotic preparations─inactivated bacterial cells (POST) and cell-free fermentation supernatant (CFS)─effectively alleviated dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis in mice. Integrated gut microbiome and serum metabolomics analyses indicated that these interventions may act through modulating bile acid metabolism and Toll-like receptor signaling pathways. Further investigations combining postbiotic metabolomics, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations identified α-muricholic acid (α-MCA) as a candidate functional metabolite, with the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) as a potential target. We hypothesize that α-MCA may contribute to ameliorating intestinal inflammation through engagement of FXR and suppression of the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway. These findings provide new insights into postbiotic-based therapeutic strategies for IBD.
